text: You already know how to compute a dot product: multiply the matching entries and add them up. You have also used cosine similarity to rank documents in a retrieval system. This lesson gives that arithmetic a picture, and the picture is a shadow.

Place two arrows, v and w, tail to tail. Imagine a light shining straight down onto the line through w, at right angles to it, so that v casts a shadow along that line. The length of that shadow is called the projection of v onto w, and it tells you how much of v points in the direction of w.

The dot product is the length of the shadow multiplied by the length of w. When the two arrows point the same way, the shadow is long and the dot product is large and positive. As v turns away, the shadow shrinks, and at a right angle it vanishes, which is why perpendicular vectors have a dot product of zero. Turn further still and the shadow falls behind the origin, so the dot product becomes negative.

Why should the multiply and add recipe produce a shadow? Write v as x steps along i hat and y steps along j hat. The shadow of a sum is the sum of the shadows, so the dot product with w splits into x times the dot product of i hat with w, plus y times the dot product of j hat with w. Those two dot products are simply the entries of w, and the familiar recipe falls out.

If w has length one, a unit vector, the dot product is the shadow itself, with no extra factor mixed in. This is why cosine similarity divides by both lengths. Once both arrows have length one, the shadow of one on the other is exactly the cosine of the angle between them, and how long the original arrows were stops mattering.

Projection also splits any vector into two pieces. One piece is the shadow along w, written as a vector pointing along w. The other is whatever is left over, and the leftover always stands at a right angle to w, because its dot product with w is zero. That clean right angle is what makes least squares regression work, which we will meet later in the course.

Inside a transformer, attention decides how much one token should listen to another by taking the dot product of a query vector with a key vector, so a long shadow means a strong match. Next, we look for the directions that a matrix leaves pointing the same way, which are called eigenvectors.
